lesson_title: The Month Written Down Before It Happens: Budgeting
hook_text: She saved R600 on marketing — and it cost her R3 200. The cheapest line on the budget was the most expensive thing she bought.
clip_script: Karabo shoots weddings and matric dances on weekends, and at the end of every month she does something her friends tease her about: she writes down NEXT month before it happens. Two lists. Will the photography make a profit — bookings, prints, travel, even the slow wearing of her camera shutters? And the harder list: will there be money in the account on the RIGHT DAYS? Because the subscription debits on the first, the taxi wants cash every Saturday, and the wedding couple only pays after the album lands on the twenty-eighth. Profitable and broke are different things — bills arrive on dates, not averages. Then month-end comes, and she sits with two columns: planned, and happened. Bookings: planned fifteen thousand, actual eleven eight. Down three thousand two hundred — why? Her eye catches the next line. Boosted posts and flyers: planned six hundred. Spent: nothing. She skipped the marketing to save money. There is the answer, staring back in two rows: she saved six hundred rand and lost three thousand two hundred in bookings. The saving was the most expensive thing she bought all month. That is the whole discipline of budgeting: write it down before, compare it after, and judge lines in PAIRS — because an underspend is not a victory until you know what the money was supposed to cause.
visual_style: A desk lamp over two handwritten columns side by side; coins sliding between a marketing line and a bookings line to show the causal pair; a calendar with debit dates lighting up in sequence.
mood: Intimate, practical, sharply illuminating at the reveal.
pacing: Quiet late-night open, calendar urgency in the middle, slow two-row reveal, firm closing rule.
